about: Mathematics 1B (ELEC40014) is the compulsory 7.5 ECTS spring-term maths module for first-year Electrical and Electronic Engineering at Imperial, following Mathematics 1A in the autumn. Its descriptor (last revised January 2025) lists the content in this order: double integration, Fourier series, Fourier transforms, Laplace transforms, multivariable calculus part 2, vectors and linear algebra, with applications in electromagnetism, signal processing and communications. Teaching is about 36 hours of recorded lectures, two problem classes a week and small-group tutorials. The descriptor gives assessment as a spring mid-term test (10%) and an exam at the start of the summer term (90%). It does not break the topics into sub-topics, so the sub-topics in each note (for example the split of multivariable calculus) are standard ones chosen by us.

notes.h: Double integrals: iterated integrals, changing order and polar coordinates
notes.body:
A double integral ∫∫_R f(x, y) dA adds up f over a region R of the plane. If f ≥ 0 it is the volume under the surface z = f(x, y); with f = 1 it is the area of R; with f a density it is a mass. In engineering you meet it for charge on a plate, moments of area and, later, probability.

Iterated integrals
- In practice you evaluate a double integral as two single integrals, one inside the other.
- Fubini's theorem (the version you need): if f is continuous on a closed, bounded region R, the double integral equals the iterated integral taken in either order, provided the limits correctly describe R.
- Type I region: a ≤ x ≤ b, g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x). Then ∫∫_R f dA = ∫ₐᵇ ( ∫ from g₁(x) to g₂(x) of f dy ) dx.
- Type II region: c ≤ y ≤ d, h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y). Integrate in x first.
- The inner limits may depend on the outer variable; the outer limits must be constants.

Worked example
Integrate f = xy over the triangle 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1.
- y first: ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ xy dy dx = ∫₀¹ x·x²/2 dx = 1/8.
- x first: for fixed y, x runs from y to 1, so ∫₀¹ ∫ᵧ¹ xy dx dy = ∫₀¹ y(1 − y²)/2 dy = 1/4 − 1/8 = 1/8. Both orders agree, as they must.

Changing the order of integration
- Always sketch R first. Read off the new limits from the sketch, not by swapping the old ones.
- Some integrals are impossible in one order but easy in the other, e.g. ∫₀¹ ∫ᵧ¹ e^(x²) dx dy: reversing gives ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ e^(x²) dy dx = ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx = (e − 1)/2.

Polar coordinates
- x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and the area element becomes dA = r dr dθ. The extra factor r is the Jacobian |∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ)| = r.
- Use polar coordinates for discs, sectors, annuli, or integrands containing x² + y².
- Example: ∫∫ over the disc x² + y² ≤ a² of e^(−(x² + y²)) dA = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀ᵃ e^(−r²) r dr dθ = π(1 − e^(−a²)). Letting a → ∞ gives π, which is how one shows ∫ e^(−x²) dx over the whole real line equals √π.

General change of variables
- For x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v), dA = |J| du dv with J = ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = x_u y_v − x_v y_u.

Applications
- Mass M = ∫∫ ρ dA; centroid x̄ = (1/A)∫∫ x dA. For a quarter disc of radius a, x̄ = ȳ = 4a/(3π).

Exam tips: sketch the region every time, write the limits before integrating, and never forget the r in polar coordinates.

A Fourier series writes a periodic function as a sum of sinusoids at multiples of a fundamental frequency. In EEE this is how you see the harmonic content of a square wave, a rectified sine or a PWM signal.

Definitions (period T, fundamental angular frequency ω₀ = 2π/T)
- f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ (n = 1 to ∞) [aₙ cos(nω₀t) + bₙ sin(nω₀t)]
- aₙ = (2/T) ∫ over one period of f(t) cos(nω₀t) dt, for n = 0, 1, 2, …
- bₙ = (2/T) ∫ over one period of f(t) sin(nω₀t) dt, for n = 1, 2, …
- With the a₀/2 convention, a₀/2 is the mean value of f over a period. Check which convention your notes use.
- For period 2π, ω₀ = 1 and the formulae have 1/π in front of an integral from −π to π.

Why the formulae work: orthogonality. Over one period, ∫ cos(mω₀t) cos(nω₀t) dt = 0 for m ≠ n, the sine–sine integrals behave the same way, and every sine–cosine product integrates to 0. Multiplying f by one basis function and integrating picks out one coefficient.

Symmetry saves work
- Even f (f(−t) = f(t)): all bₙ = 0, so it is a cosine series.
- Odd f (f(−t) = −f(t)): all aₙ = 0 (including a₀), so it is a sine series.
- For odd or even f you can integrate over half a period and double the result.

Worked examples (period 2π)
- f(x) = x on (−π, π): odd, so aₙ = 0. Integration by parts gives bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x sin nx dx = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n. So x = 2(sin x − sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 − …).
- Square wave, f = −1 on (−π, 0) and +1 on (0, π): bₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n and 0 for even n, so f = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + …). Only odd harmonics appear, with amplitudes falling like 1/n.

Convergence (Dirichlet conditions)
If f is periodic, piecewise continuous with finitely many jumps and finitely many maxima and minima in a period, and absolutely integrable over a period, then its Fourier series converges to f(t) wherever f is continuous and to the average [f(t⁻) + f(t⁺)]/2 at a jump. So the square-wave series gives 0 at x = 0.

Gibbs phenomenon: near a jump, partial sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump size, however many terms you take. The overshoot narrows but does not shrink.

Complex form: f(t) = Σ cₙ e^(jnω₀t) over all integers n, with cₙ = (1/T)∫ f(t) e^(−jnω₀t) dt. For real f, c₋ₙ is the complex conjugate of cₙ, and aₙ = 2 Re cₙ, bₙ = −2 Im cₙ.

Parseval's theorem (mean power): (1/T)∫ f² dt = a₀²/4 + ½ Σ (aₙ² + bₙ²) = Σ |cₙ|². Applied to f = x on (−π, π) it gives Σ 1/n² = π²/6.

Exam tips: state the period and ω₀ first, use symmetry before integrating, and remember (−1)ⁿ = cos nπ.

notes.h: The Fourier transform of non-periodic signals
notes.body:
A Fourier series describes a periodic signal with discrete frequencies nω₀. Letting the period T → ∞, the spacing ω₀ shrinks to zero and the sum becomes an integral: the Fourier transform, which gives a continuous spectrum for a pulse or other non-periodic signal.

Definition (the usual EEE convention, with j² = −1)
- F(ω) = ∫ f(t) e^(−jωt) dt over all t
- f(t) = (1/2π) ∫ F(ω) e^(jωt) dω over all ω
- Some books put the 1/2π elsewhere or use frequency f in Hz (ω = 2πf). Use the convention in your formula sheet consistently.
- A sufficient condition for F to exist is that f is absolutely integrable: ∫|f(t)| dt < ∞.

Standard pairs
- Rectangular pulse of height 1 on |t| < T/2: F(ω) = 2 sin(ωT/2)/ω = T sinc(ωT/2), where sinc x = sin x / x. F(0) = T, the pulse area, and the first zeros are at ω = ±2π/T.
- e^(−at)u(t), with a > 0 and u the unit step: F(ω) = 1/(a + jω).
- e^(−a|t|), with a > 0: F(ω) = 2a/(a² + ω²).
- δ(t): F(ω) = 1, so an impulse contains all frequencies equally.

Properties (if f ↔ F)
- Linearity: af + bg ↔ aF + bG.
- Time shift: f(t − t₀) ↔ e^(−jωt₀)F(ω). Only the phase changes; |F| is unchanged.
- Frequency shift (modulation): e^(jω₀t)f(t) ↔ F(ω − ω₀). Hence f(t)cos ω₀t ↔ ½[F(ω − ω₀) + F(ω + ω₀)], the basis of AM.
- Scaling: f(at) ↔ (1/|a|)F(ω/a). Squeezing in time spreads in frequency.
- Differentiation: f′(t) ↔ jωF(ω), if f → 0 as |t| → ∞.
- Convolution: (f * g)(t) ↔ F(ω)G(ω). For a linear time-invariant system, output spectrum = H(ω) × input spectrum.
- Duality: if f(t) ↔ F(ω), then F(t) ↔ 2πf(−ω).

Energy (Parseval/Rayleigh)
∫|f(t)|² dt = (1/2π)∫|F(ω)|² dω. Example: f = e^(−at)u(t) has energy ∫₀^∞ e^(−2at) dt = 1/(2a). On the frequency side, (1/2π)∫ dω/(a² + ω²) = (1/2π)(π/a) = 1/(2a), as it should.

Worked example
A pulse of height A on 0 < t < τ is the centred pulse delayed by τ/2, so F(ω) = e^(−jωτ/2) · 2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω. Its magnitude is the same as for the centred pulse.

Exam tips: write every new transform as a known pair plus a property (shift, scale, modulate), and check F(0) = ∫ f dt as a quick test.

The Laplace transform turns linear differential equations with constant coefficients into algebra in a complex variable s. It handles initial conditions automatically and leads to transfer functions in circuits and control.

Definition: F(s) = L{f(t)} = ∫₀^∞ f(t) e^(−st) dt, for Re(s) large enough that the integral converges. Only t ≥ 0 matters.

Table you should know
- 1 (or u(t)) → 1/s
- tⁿ → n!/s^(n+1)
- e^(at) → 1/(s − a)
- sin ωt → ω/(s² + ω²); cos ωt → s/(s² + ω²)
- δ(t) → 1

Key properties
- Linearity.
- First shift theorem: L{e^(at)f(t)} = F(s − a). Example: L{t e^(−2t)} = 1/(s + 2)².
- Second shift (delay): L{f(t − T)u(t − T)} = e^(−sT)F(s), for T > 0.
- Derivatives: L{f′} = sF(s) − f(0); L{f″} = s²F(s) − s f(0) − f′(0).
- Convolution: L{(f * g)(t)} = F(s)G(s), with (f * g)(t) = ∫₀ᵗ f(τ)g(t − τ) dτ. Note that the transform of a product f·g is NOT F·G.

Initial and final value theorems
- Initial value: f(0⁺) = lim (s → ∞) sF(s), provided this limit exists.
- Final value: if all poles of sF(s) lie in the open left half-plane (Re s < 0), then lim (t → ∞) f(t) = lim (s → 0) sF(s). A single pole of F at s = 0 is allowed, because it cancels with the factor s. If sF(s) has poles on the imaginary axis or in the right half-plane, f(t) has no limit and the theorem must not be used.

Method for an ODE
1. Transform both sides, substituting the initial conditions.
2. Solve for Y(s).
3. Split into partial fractions and invert using the table.

Worked example: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 2, y(0) = y′(0) = 0
- (s² + 3s + 2)Y = 2/s, so Y = 2/[s(s + 1)(s + 2)].
- Partial fractions: Y = 1/s − 2/(s + 1) + 1/(s + 2).
- y(t) = 1 − 2e^(−t) + e^(−2t). Check: y(0) = 0, and y → 1, which agrees with the final value theorem: sY → 2/2 = 1.

Complex poles: complete the square. For example (s + 2)/[(s + 1)² + 4] = (s + 1)/[(s + 1)² + 4] + ½ · 2/[(s + 1)² + 4], which inverts to e^(−t)cos 2t + ½e^(−t) sin 2t.

Transfer functions: with zero initial conditions, H(s) = Y(s)/X(s). Poles in the left half-plane give decaying (stable) responses. For a series RC circuit with the output across C, H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC).

Exam tips: show the partial-fraction constants clearly, check y(0) from your answer, and check the final value theorem's hypothesis before you use it.

notes.h: Multivariable calculus: chain rule, Taylor series and optimisation
notes.body:
This part builds on partial derivatives (from the first half of the year's maths) and applies them to rates of change, approximation and optimisation. (The descriptor only says 'Multivariable calculus part 2'; the sub-topics below are the standard ones and may be split differently in your lectures.)

Chain rule
- If z = f(x, y) with x = x(t) and y = y(t), then dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt.
- If x = x(u, v) and y = y(u, v), then ∂z/∂u = f_x ∂x/∂u + f_y ∂y/∂u, and similarly for v.
- Example: z = x²y, x = cos t, y = sin t. At t = π/4, f_x = 2xy = 1, f_y = x² = ½, dx/dt = −1/√2, dy/dt = 1/√2. So dz/dt = −1/√2 + 1/(2√2) = −1/(2√2) ≈ −0.354.

Total differential and error estimates
- dz = f_x dx + f_y dy approximates the change in z for small changes dx and dy.
- For a product z = xy, the relative errors add: dz/z = dx/x + dy/y. So a 1% error in each factor gives at most about 2% in the product.

Gradient and directional derivative
- ∇f = (f_x, f_y). The rate of change in the direction of a unit vector û is ∇f · û.
- ∇f points in the direction of steepest increase and is perpendicular to the level curves f = constant.

Taylor series in two variables (about (a, b), with h = x − a, k = y − b)
f(a + h, b + k) ≈ f + h f_x + k f_y + ½(h² f_xx + 2hk f_xy + k² f_yy), all derivatives taken at (a, b). Example: e^x cos y ≈ 1 + x + ½(x² − y²) near the origin.

Stationary points
- Stationary point: f_x = f_y = 0.
- Second-derivative test (f with continuous second partial derivatives near the point): let D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)².
  - D > 0 and f_xx > 0: local minimum.
  - D > 0 and f_xx < 0: local maximum.
  - D < 0: saddle point.
  - D = 0: the test is inconclusive.
- Example: f = x³ − 3x + y². Then f_x = 3x² − 3 and f_y = 2y, so the stationary points are (1, 0) and (−1, 0). With f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 2 and f_xy = 0: at (1, 0), D = 12 > 0 and f_xx > 0, a minimum; at (−1, 0), D = −12, a saddle.

Lagrange multipliers
- Theorem: suppose f and g have continuous first partial derivatives, and f, restricted to the curve g(x, y) = c, has a local extremum at a point where ∇g ≠ 0. Then ∇f = λ∇g at that point for some λ.
- Method: solve f_x = λg_x, f_y = λg_y, g = c, then compare the values of f at the candidates.
- Example: extremise x + y on x² + y² = 2. Then 1 = 2λx and 1 = 2λy, so x = y = ±1. The maximum is 2 at (1, 1) and the minimum is −2 at (−1, −1).

Exam tips: list every stationary point before classifying it, and in Lagrange problems state the constraint and check ∇g ≠ 0.

notes.h: Vectors: products, lines, planes and vector fields
notes.body:
Vectors carry the geometry behind electromagnetism (forces, fields, flux) and much of signal processing. You need fluent component calculations and the geometric meaning of each product.

Dot (scalar) product
- a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ.
- a · b = 0 for non-zero vectors means they are perpendicular. The component of a along b is a · b / |b|.
- Example: a = (1, 2, 2), b = (3, 0, 4). Then a · b = 11, |a| = 3, |b| = 5, so cos θ = 11/15.

Cross (vector) product
- a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁), the determinant with rows i j k / a / b.
- |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram on a and b. The direction is perpendicular to both, by the right-hand rule.
- b × a = −(a × b). a × a = 0.
- Example: (1, 2, 2) × (3, 0, 4) = (8, 2, −6). Check: dotting with either vector gives 0.
- Physics: the force on a charge is F = q(E + v × B), and torque is τ = r × F.

Triple products
- Scalar triple product a · (b × c) = det[a; b; c]. Its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped. It is zero exactly when the three vectors are coplanar.
- Vector triple product: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.

Lines and planes
- Line through point A with direction d: r = a + λd.
- Plane with normal n: r · n = d, or n₁x + n₂y + n₃z = d.
- Distance from point P to that plane: |n · p − d| / |n|.
- Example: the distance from (1, 1, 1) to 2x − y + 2z = 9 is |2 − 1 + 2 − 9|/3 = 2.
- Line meets plane: substitute r = a + λd into the plane equation and solve for λ.

Scalar and vector fields (for electromagnetism)
- Gradient of a scalar φ: ∇φ = (φ_x, φ_y, φ_z), normal to the level surfaces. For example E = −∇V.
- Divergence of F = (F₁, F₂, F₃): ∇ · F = ∂F₁/∂x + ∂F₂/∂y + ∂F₃/∂z, the net outflow per unit volume.
- Curl: ∇ × F, the determinant with rows i j k / ∂/∂x ∂/∂y ∂/∂z / F₁ F₂ F₃. It measures local rotation.
- Identities (for fields with continuous second derivatives): ∇ × (∇φ) = 0 and ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.
- Example: F = (xy, yz, zx) has ∇ · F = y + z + x and ∇ × F = (−y, −z, −x).

Exam tips: check a cross product by dotting it with both factors, and keep the minus sign on the middle component of the determinant expansion.

notes.h: Linear algebra: systems, determinants and eigenvalues
notes.body:
Linear algebra organises many simultaneous equations into one object. Circuit analysis (nodal and mesh equations), state-space models and signal processing all reduce to matrix problems.

Matrices and determinants
- The product AB is defined when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. In general AB ≠ BA.
- 2 × 2: det [[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc, and the inverse is (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]] when ad − bc ≠ 0.
- 3 × 3: expand along any row or column with the sign pattern + − + / − + − / + − +.
- Useful facts: det(AB) = det A det B; det(Aᵀ) = det A; swapping two rows changes the sign; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged.
- A square A is invertible if and only if det A ≠ 0.

Solving Ax = b by Gaussian elimination
- Reduce the augmented matrix [A | b] to row echelon form using row operations, then back-substitute.
- Example: 2x + y − z = 8, −3x − y + 2z = −11, −2x + y + 2z = −3 has the unique solution x = 2, y = 3, z = −1.

How many solutions? (A is m × n)
- The system is consistent if and only if rank A = rank [A | b].
- If consistent: a unique solution when rank A = n; infinitely many when rank A < n (n − rank free parameters).
- For square A: det A ≠ 0 gives a unique solution for every b. If det A = 0 there is either no solution or infinitely many, depending on b.
- Example: x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 2x + 3y + 4z = m. The third row of A is the sum of the first two, so det A = 0 and rank A = 2. The system is consistent only when m = 1 + 2 = 3, and then it has infinitely many solutions.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
- v ≠ 0 is an eigenvector of square A with eigenvalue λ if Av = λv.
- The eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. For each λ, the eigenvectors are the non-zero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0.
- Checks: the sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace, and their product equals det A.
- Example: A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]] gives λ² − 7λ + 10 = 0, so λ = 2 or 5.
- Triangular matrices have their diagonal entries as eigenvalues. This is not true in general.

Diagonalisation
- If the n × n matrix A has n linearly independent eigenvectors (guaranteed when the n eigenvalues are distinct), then P⁻¹AP = D, where the columns of P are the eigenvectors and D = diag(λ₁, …, λₙ).
- Real symmetric matrices always have real eigenvalues and can be diagonalised with orthogonal eigenvectors.
- Example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has λ = 1 with v = (1, −1) and λ = 3 with v = (1, 1).
- Use: Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹, which makes powers easy to compute.

Exam tips: check eigenvalues against the trace and determinant, and check each eigenvector by computing Av.

rank A = rank [A | b].

cards.f: Infinitely many solutions (A is m × n, system consistent)
cards.b: rank A < n; there are n − rank A free parameters.
det(A − λI) = 0; its roots are the eigenvalues.

cards.f: Trace and determinant checks on eigenvalues
cards.b: Sum of eigenvalues = trace A; product of eigenvalues = det A.
When it has n linearly independent eigenvectors; n distinct eigenvalues are enough. Real symmetric matrices always are.
1 (eigenvector (1, −1)) and 3 (eigenvector (1, 1)).

cards.f: Effect of row operations on det
cards.b: Swapping two rows changes the sign; scaling a row by k multiplies det by k; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫∫_D (x² + y²) dA, where D is the unit disc x² + y² ≤ 1.
questions.why: In polar coordinates the integral is ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀¹ r²·r dr dθ = 2π × 1/4 = π/2. The answer 2π/3 comes from leaving out the Jacobian r, giving ∫ r² dr = 1/3 instead of 1/4. π/4 comes from letting θ run only from 0 to π (half the disc). 1/4 is the r-integral alone, forgetting to multiply by the 2π from the θ-integral.

questions.q: Which iterated integral equals ∫₀¹ ∫ₓ¹ f(x, y) dy dx?
questions.why: The region is x ≤ y ≤ 1 with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, i.e. the triangle above the line y = x. For fixed y, x runs from 0 to y, giving ∫₀¹ ∫₀ʸ f dx dy. The version with x from y to 1 describes the triangle below y = x, the result of swapping the limits without sketching. The integral over the full square ignores the line y = x altogether. Keeping inner limits from x to 1 while integrating in x first is meaningless, because the inner limits then contain the variable being integrated.

questions.q: The region R lies between the curves y = x² and y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. (a) Write ∫∫_R (x + y) dA as an iterated integral in both orders. (b) Evaluate it.
markScheme: Correct sketch: y = x lies above y = x² on 0 < x < 1; they meet at (0, 0) and (1, 1)
y-first form: ∫₀¹ ∫ from x² to x of (x + y) dy dx
x-first form: ∫₀¹ ∫ from y to √y of (x + y) dx dy
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 the line y = x lies above the parabola y = x², so R = {0 ≤ x ≤ 1, x² ≤ y ≤ x}. In the other order, for 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, x runs from the line (x = y) to the parabola (x = √y). So the integral is ∫₀¹ ∫ from x² to x of (x + y) dy dx = ∫₀¹ ∫ from y to √y of (x + y) dx dy.
(b) Inner integral: [xy + y²/2] from x² to x = x² − x³ + (x² − x⁴)/2. Integrate from 0 to 1: 1/3 − 1/4 + 1/6 − 1/10 = (20 − 15 + 10 − 6)/60 = 9/60 = 3/20.

questions.q: The square wave f(x) = −1 for −π < x < 0, f(x) = 1 for 0 < x < π, period 2π, has Fourier series (4/π)Σ sin(nx)/n over odd n. What value does the series take at x = 0?
questions.why: At a jump the series converges to the average of the one-sided limits, (−1 + 1)/2 = 0; every term sin(n·0) is zero, which confirms it. The value 1 is the right-hand limit only, and −1 the left-hand limit only. About 1.18 is the peak of the partial sums just to the right of the jump (the Gibbs overshoot of about 9% of the jump of 2, i.e. (2/π)Si(π) ≈ 1.179); that peak occurs near the jump in partial sums, not at the jump in the full series.

questions.q: For f(x) = x on (−π, π), extended with period 2π, what is bₙ?
questions.why: bₙ = (1/π)∫ x sin nx dx over (−π, π) = (2/π)∫₀^π x sin nx dx. By parts this is (2/π)(−π cos nπ / n) = −2(−1)ⁿ/n = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n, so b₁ = 2. The form 2(−1)ⁿ/n has the sign slip from dropping the minus sign in the parts formula. (−1)^(n+1)/n is what you get if you integrate only over (0, π) without doubling, i.e. forget that x sin nx is even. All coefficients 0 mixes up which coefficients vanish: for an odd function it is the aₙ that are zero, not the bₙ.

questions.q: Find the Fourier series of the square wave f(x) = −1 for −π < x < 0, f(x) = 1 for 0 < x < π, period 2π. State which harmonics are present.
markScheme: f is odd, so aₙ = 0 for all n
bₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n, 0 for even n
Series (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + …): only odd harmonics
questions.modelAnswer: f is odd, so every aₙ is zero. Then bₙ = (1/π)∫ f sin nx dx over (−π, π) = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = (2/(nπ))[−cos nx]₀^π = (2/(nπ))(1 − (−1)ⁿ). This is 4/(nπ) when n is odd and 0 when n is even. So f(x) = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + …): only odd harmonics appear, with amplitudes falling like 1/n.

questions.q: If f(t) has Fourier transform F(ω), what is the Fourier transform of f(t − 3)?
questions.why: A delay of t₀ multiplies the transform by e^(−jωt₀), so a delay of 3 gives e^(−3jω)F(ω). The factor e^(3jω) has the wrong sign; it belongs to an advance, f(t + 3). F(ω − 3) is the frequency-shift (modulation) rule, which applies to e^(3jt)f(t), not to a delay. 3F(3ω) mixes the delay up with a scaling rule, and is not even the correct form of that rule.

questions.q: If f(t) has Fourier transform F(ω), what is the Fourier transform of f(2t)?
questions.why: Substituting u = 2t gives ∫ f(u) e^(−jωu/2) du/2 = ½F(ω/2): compressing in time stretches the spectrum and scales it by 1/|a|. The form 2F(2ω) applies the scaling rule the wrong way round. F(ω/2) has the right argument but drops the 1/|a| factor from the change of variable du = 2 dt. ½F(2ω) has the right factor but the inverted argument.

questions.q: (a) Find the Fourier transform of the pulse p(t) = A for |t| < τ/2, p(t) = 0 otherwise. (b) Hence find the transform of q(t) = A for 0 < t < τ, 0 otherwise, and state |Q(ω)|.
markScheme: P(ω) = ∫ from −τ/2 to τ/2 of A e^(−jωt) dt
= 2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω (= Aτ sinc(ωτ/2)), with P(0) = Aτ
|Q(ω)| = |2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω|: delay changes only the phase
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) P(ω) = ∫ from −τ/2 to τ/2 of A e^(−jωt) dt = A[e^(−jωt)/(−jω)] = (A/(jω))(e^(jωτ/2) − e^(−jωτ/2)) = 2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω, which equals Aτ sinc(ωτ/2) and tends to Aτ (the area) as ω → 0.
(b) q is p delayed by τ/2, so Q(ω) = e^(−jωτ/2) · 2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω. Since |e^(−jωτ/2)| = 1, |Q(ω)| = |2A sin(ωτ/2)/ω|, the same as |P(ω)|; only the phase differs.

questions.q: What is the Laplace transform of t e^(−2t)?
questions.why: L{t} = 1/s², and multiplying by e^(−2t) replaces s with s + 2 (first shift theorem with a = −2), giving 1/(s + 2)². 1/(s − 2)² uses the wrong sign of the shift; that is the transform of t e^(2t). 1/[s²(s + 2)] multiplies the two transforms, but a product of transforms corresponds to a convolution, not to a product of functions. 2/(s + 2)³ uses n!/s^(n+1) with n = 2, which is the transform of t² e^(−2t).

questions.q: A signal has F(s) = (s + 5)/[s(s + 2)]. What is lim f(t) as t → ∞?
options: It does not exist, because F has a pole at s = 0
questions.why: sF(s) = (s + 5)/(s + 2) has its only pole at s = −2, in the left half-plane, so the final value theorem applies: lim sF(s) as s → 0 is 5/2. (Indeed f(t) = 5/2 − (3/2)e^(−2t).) The value 1 is lim sF(s) as s → ∞, which is the initial value f(0⁺), not the final value. 0 assumes that every term of f(t) dies away, but the pole of F at s = 0 contributes the constant 5/2; it is also what you get from lim F(s) as s → ∞, leaving out the factor s. A simple pole of F at s = 0 does not stop the theorem: it cancels with the s, and it is precisely what produces the constant final value.

questions.q: Use the Laplace transform to solve y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 2 with y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 0, and confirm the limit of y(t) as t → ∞ with the final value theorem.
markScheme: sY(s) → 1 as s → 0, and the poles of sY are −1 and −2 (left half-plane), so y → 1
questions.modelAnswer: With zero initial conditions, L{y″} = s²Y and L{y′} = sY, so (s² + 3s + 2)Y = 2/s and Y = 2/[s(s + 1)(s + 2)]. Cover-up: at s = 0 the coefficient is 2/(1·2) = 1; at s = −1 it is 2/((−1)(1)) = −2; at s = −2 it is 2/((−2)(−1)) = 1. So Y = 1/s − 2/(s + 1) + 1/(s + 2) and y(t) = 1 − 2e^(−t) + e^(−2t). Check: y(0) = 1 − 2 + 1 = 0. sY(s) = 2/[(s + 1)(s + 2)] has poles at −1 and −2 only, so the final value theorem applies and gives lim y = 2/2 = 1, matching the solution.

questions.q: Classify the stationary point of f(x, y) = x² + 4xy + y² at the origin.
questions.why: f_xx = 2, f_yy = 2 and f_xy = 4, so D = 2·2 − 4² = −12 < 0, which is a saddle (along y = −x, f = −2x² < 0). Local minimum comes from looking only at f_xx > 0 and f_yy > 0 and ignoring the cross term. Local maximum misreads the rule, treating D < 0 as a maximum. D = 0 results from taking f_xy = 2, half the coefficient of xy, instead of differentiating 4xy to get 4.

questions.q: z = x²y with x = cos t, y = sin t. What is dz/dt at t = π/4?
questions.why: At t = π/4, x = y = 1/√2, so f_x = 2xy = 1 and f_y = x² = ½, with dx/dt = −1/√2 and dy/dt = 1/√2. dz/dt = 1·(−1/√2) + ½·(1/√2) = −1/(2√2). −1/√2 keeps only the f_x dx/dt term. 1/(2√2) keeps only the f_y dy/dt term. 3/(2√2) comes from taking d(cos t)/dt as +sin t, which flips the sign of the first term.

questions.q: Find and classify the stationary points of f(x, y) = x³ − 3x + y².
questions.modelAnswer: f_x = 3x² − 3 and f_y = 2y. Setting both to zero gives x = ±1 and y = 0, so the stationary points are (1, 0) and (−1, 0). Second derivatives: f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 0, so D = 12x. At (1, 0), D = 12 > 0 and f_xx = 6 > 0: a local minimum with f = 1 − 3 = −2. At (−1, 0), D = −12 < 0: a saddle point, with f = −1 + 3 = 2.

questions.q: What is a × b for a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (3, 0, 4)?
questions.why: a × b = (2·4 − 2·0, 2·3 − 1·4, 1·0 − 2·3) = (8, 2, −6); dotting it with a gives 8 + 4 − 12 = 0, as it should. (8, −2, −6) comes from expanding the determinant but forgetting the minus sign on the j-cofactor. (−8, −2, 6) is b × a, from taking the vectors in the wrong order. (3, 0, 8) multiplies matching components, which is not a vector product at all (they are the terms that sum to the dot product).

questions.q: What is the distance from the point (1, 1, 1) to the plane 2x − y + 2z = 9?
questions.why: Distance = |n · p − d|/|n| = |2 − 1 + 2 − 9|/√(4 + 1 + 4) = 6/3 = 2. 6 leaves out the division by |n|. 2/3 divides by |n|² = 9 instead of |n| = 3. 1 leaves out d, i.e. computes |n · p|/|n| = 3/3, which is the distance to the parallel plane through the origin.

questions.q: The line r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(1, 1, −1) meets the plane 2x − y + 2z = 9. (a) Find the point of intersection. (b) Find the angle between the line and the normal to the plane.
markScheme: Point (−2, −3, 5), checked in the plane equation
Angle with the normal ≈ 101.1° (equivalently ≈ 78.9° between the line and the normal direction −n)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A point on the line is (1 + λ, λ, 2 − λ). Substituting: 2 + 2λ − λ + 4 − 2λ = 6 − λ = 9, so λ = −3 and the point is (−2, −3, 5). Check: −4 + 3 + 10 = 9.
(b) d = (1, 1, −1) and n = (2, −1, 2), so d · n = 2 − 1 − 2 = −1, |d| = √3 and |n| = 3. cos φ = −1/(3√3) ≈ −0.192, so φ ≈ 101.1°. Equivalently the acute angle between the line and the normal line is ≈ 78.9°, so the line makes about 11.1° with the plane itself.

questions.q: What are the eigenvalues of A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]?
questions.why: det(A − λI) = (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − 2 = λ² − 7λ + 10 = (λ − 2)(λ − 5), so λ = 2 and 5 (sum 7 = trace, product 10 = det). 4 and 3 are the diagonal entries, which are eigenvalues only for triangular matrices. −2 and −5 come from a sign slip when reading roots off the factorised quadratic. 7 and 10 are the trace and determinant, i.e. the sum and product of the eigenvalues, not the eigenvalues themselves.

questions.q: For the system x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 2x + 3y + 4z = m, which statement is correct?
options: There is no solution exactly when m ≠ 3
There is no solution exactly when m = 3
There is a unique solution for every m, because there are three equations in three unknowns
There is no solution for any m, because det A = 0
questions.why: The third row of A is the sum of the first two, so det A = 0 and rank A = 2. The system is consistent only if the right-hand sides match the same relation, i.e. m = 1 + 2 = 3; then there are infinitely many solutions, and for m ≠ 3 there are none. Saying no solution when m = 3 reverses the consistent and inconsistent cases. Equal numbers of equations and unknowns do not guarantee a unique solution; that needs det A ≠ 0. det A = 0 does not always mean no solution: when the right-hand side is consistent there are infinitely many.

questions.q: Let A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. (a) Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. (b) Write down P and D with P⁻¹AP = D. (c) Hence find A¹⁰ (you may leave powers of 3 unevaluated).
markScheme: A¹⁰ = P D¹⁰ P⁻¹ with P⁻¹ = ½[[1, −1], [1, 1]]
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0 gives 2 − λ = ±1, so λ = 1 or 3. For λ = 1: (A − I)v = 0 gives v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, −1). For λ = 3: −v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, 1).
(b) P = [[1, 1], [−1, 1]] (columns are the eigenvectors), D = diag(1, 3).
(c) P⁻¹ = ½[[1, −1], [1, 1]]. A¹⁰ = P diag(1, 3¹⁰) P⁻¹ = ½[[1 + 3¹⁰, 3¹⁰ − 1], [3¹⁰ − 1, 1 + 3¹⁰]]. Check with power 1: ½[[4, 2], [2, 4]] = A.

questions.q:
The function f(t) = t for −π < t < π is extended to be periodic with period 2π.
(a) Explain, using symmetry, which Fourier coefficients vanish. [2]
(b) Show that the Fourier series is f(t) = Σ (n = 1 to ∞) 2(−1)^(n+1) sin(nt)/n. [6]
(c) State, with a reason, the value of the series at t = π, and sketch the sum of the series on −3π < t < 3π. [4]
(d) Use Parseval's theorem to show that Σ 1/n² = π²/6. [5]
(e) Explain what a plot of a partial sum looks like near t = π, and why this matters if the series is used to synthesise a sawtooth signal. [3]
markScheme: (a) f is odd, so aₙ = 0 for all n including a₀; only sine terms remain
(b) bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π t sin nt dt, integration by parts done correctly
(c) At t = π there is a jump from π to −π; the series converges to the average 0 (Dirichlet), consistent with every sin(nπ) = 0; sketch is a sawtooth with midpoints at the jumps
(d) (1/2π)∫ t² dt = π²/3 on the left; ½Σbₙ² = 2Σ1/n² on the right
(e) Gibbs phenomenon: overshoot of about 9% of the jump (jump 2π) near t = π that narrows but does not vanish; ringing in a synthesised signal
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) f(−t) = −f(t), so f is odd. f(t)cos nt is then odd and integrates to zero over (−π, π), so aₙ = 0 for every n, including a₀. Only sine terms remain.

(b) bₙ = (1/π)∫ from −π to π of t sin nt dt = (2/π)∫₀^π t sin nt dt, because t sin nt is even. By parts with u = t and dv = sin nt dt: ∫₀^π t sin nt dt = [−t cos nt / n]₀^π + (1/n)∫₀^π cos nt dt = −π cos nπ / n + 0. So bₙ = (2/π)(−π(−1)ⁿ/n) = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n, which gives f(t) = 2(sin t − sin 2t/2 + sin 3t/3 − …).

(c) The periodic extension jumps from π (as t → π⁻) to −π (as t → π⁺). Under the Dirichlet conditions (f is piecewise smooth with one jump per period) the series converges to the average, (π + (−π))/2 = 0. This agrees with the series directly, since sin(nπ) = 0 for every n. The sketch is a sawtooth rising with slope 1 from −π to π on each interval (−π + 2kπ, π + 2kπ), with dots at height 0 at t = ±π, ±3π.

(d) Parseval for period 2π: (1/2π)∫ f² dt = a₀²/4 + ½Σ(aₙ² + bₙ²). Left side: (1/2π)∫ from −π to π of t² dt = (1/2π)(2π³/3) = π²/3. Right side: ½Σ 4/n² = 2Σ1/n². So 2Σ1/n² = π²/3, giving Σ1/n² = π²/6.

(e) Near t = π, partial sums show the Gibbs phenomenon. They overshoot the true value by about 9% of the jump (the jump is 2π, so by about 0.18π) just before the discontinuity, with oscillations either side. Adding more terms squeezes the ripple closer to the jump, but its peak height does not fall. A sawtooth built from a finite number of harmonics will therefore always show ringing and overshoot at its edges.

questions.q:
A system with input x(t) and output y(t) obeys y″ + 2y′ + 5y = x(t). The system is initially at rest (y(0) = y′(0) = 0) and x(t) = 10u(t), where u is the unit step.
(a) Find the transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) and its poles. Is the system stable? [4]
(b) Find Y(s), and use the final value theorem, after checking that it applies, to find the steady-state output. [4]
(c) Find y(t) by partial fractions. [8]
(d) Find the time of the first maximum of y(t) and the percentage overshoot. [4]
markScheme: (a) H(s) = 1/(s² + 2s + 5); poles s = −1 ± 2j, in the left half-plane, so stable
(b) Y(s) = 10/[s(s² + 2s + 5)]; poles of sY are −1 ± 2j, so the final value theorem applies; y(∞) = 10/5 = 2
(d) y′(t) = 5e^(−t) sin 2t, first zero for t > 0 at t = π/2
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With zero initial conditions, (s² + 2s + 5)Y = X, so H(s) = 1/(s² + 2s + 5). The poles solve s² + 2s + 5 = 0: s = −1 ± 2j. Both have negative real part, so the system is stable (its natural response decays like e^(−t)).

(b) X(s) = 10/s, so Y(s) = 10/[s(s² + 2s + 5)]. sY(s) = 10/(s² + 2s + 5) has poles only at −1 ± 2j, in the open left half-plane, so the final value theorem applies: y(∞) = lim sY(s) as s → 0 = 10/5 = 2.

(c) Write Y = A/s + (Bs + C)/(s² + 2s + 5). Then A = 10/5 = 2. Matching numerators, 10 = 2(s² + 2s + 5) + (Bs + C)s: the s² terms give B = −2 and the s terms give 4 + C = 0, so C = −4. So Y = 2/s − (2s + 4)/[(s + 1)² + 4]. Completing the square: 2s + 4 = 2(s + 1) + 2, so Y = 2/s − 2(s + 1)/[(s + 1)² + 4] − 2/[(s + 1)² + 4]. Using the shift theorem with cos 2t ↔ s/(s² + 4) and sin 2t ↔ 2/(s² + 4):
y(t) = 2 − 2e^(−t)cos 2t − e^(−t) sin 2t, for t ≥ 0.
Check: y(0) = 2 − 2 = 0, and y → 2 as t → ∞, as found in (b).

(d) sY(s) − y(0) = 10/[(s + 1)² + 4] = 5 · 2/[(s + 1)² + 4], so y′(t) = 5e^(−t) sin 2t. (Differentiating the answer to (c) directly gives the same.) y′ = 0 first for t > 0 when 2t = π, i.e. t = π/2 ≈ 1.571. There y = 2 − 2e^(−π/2)cos π − 0 = 2 + 2e^(−π/2) ≈ 2.416. The overshoot is (2.416 − 2)/2 = e^(−π/2) ≈ 0.208, i.e. about 20.8%.
